TypeScript & Node.js Fundamentals

Always Be Compiling

TypeScript checks the deal before it closes. Node runs the room. The event loop decides who gets called next. This section moves from basic typing into project builds, generics, Node internals, module systems and npm.

1

Introduction to TypeScript: put types on the board

TypeScript adds compile-time type information to JavaScript. The compiler checks those types before Node ever sees the generated JavaScript.

ABC: Always Be Checking

A — AnnotateAdd types to variables, parameters and returns.
B — BuildRun tsc and let the compiler reject bad deals.
C — CompileTypes disappear; JavaScript is what actually runs.
D — Don't reach for anyany opts out of the protection you just added.

Primitive annotations

Types appear after the variable name:

Primitive types 
const username: string = "alice";
const attemptCount: number = 3;
const isLockedOut: boolean = false;

Assigning a different type becomes a compile error instead of a runtime surprise.

Typed functions

Parameters carry types, and the return type appears after the closing parenthesis:

Typed function 
function describeOutcome(
  outcome: string
): string {{
  return outcome === "success"
    ? "logged in successfully"
    : "failed to log in";
}}

Compare that to Java's String describeOutcome(String outcome): same information, different order.

Interfaces name an object shape

Interface 
interface Attempt {{
  username: string;
  outcome: string;
}}

const attempt: Attempt = {{
  username: "alice",
  outcome: "success"
}};

The interface closes a gap plain JavaScript leaves open: a typo like outcom can now be caught before execution.

Type erasure: TypeScript's types exist for tsc. After compilation, those annotations are removed. Node executes ordinary JavaScript and does not enforce the TypeScript types at runtime.

Inference

TypeScript often infers the type without an explicit annotation:

Type inference 
let username = "alice"; // inferred string
username = "bob";       // fine

const attemptCount = 3; // inferred from 3

any is the escape hatch

any 
let riskyValue: any = "alice";
riskyValue = 42; // no compiler complaint

any disables type checking for that value. Sometimes necessary, but it should not become the default.

Quiz hint

Be ready to distinguish compile-time checking from runtime behavior. TypeScript can catch a bug before execution, but the generated JavaScript does not retain those type annotations.

2

The TypeScript build process: close the build, not just the file

One-file compiler commands do not scale. A real project needs a project layout, a tsconfig.json, generated output and repeatable npm scripts.

Project layout

Project structure 
src/
  attempt.ts
  index.ts

dist/
  attempt.js
  attempt.d.ts
  attempt.js.map
  index.js
  index.d.ts
  index.js.map

tsconfig.json
package.json

src/ is authored code. dist/ is generated output and should not be edited by hand.

Core tsconfig settings

tsconfig.json 
{{
  "compilerOptions": {{
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "moduleResolution": "NodeNext",
    "rootDir": "src",
    "outDir": "dist",
    "strict": true,
    "declaration": true,
    "sourceMap": true
  }},
  "include": ["src/**/*"]
}}

strict enables the family of stricter checks. declaration produces .d.ts files. sourceMap produces maps between generated JS and the TS source.

NodeNext gotcha: when compiling ES-module style TypeScript for Node, an import may need to say ./attempt.js even though the source file on disk is attempt.ts. The path describes where the compiled module will be.
NodeNext import 
import {{
  describeAttempt,
  type Attempt
}} from "./attempt.js";

Build for shipping

Build and run 
npm run build
npm run start

npm run build runs tsc in project mode and writes compiled output to dist/.

Use tsx while developing

Development run 
npm run dev
# scripts.dev -> tsx src/index.ts

tsx compiles in memory and runs directly. It speeds up development but does not replace the real build for something that ships.

Quiz hint

A broken relative import can be a runtime failure under a weak configuration and a compile-time failure once NodeNext resolution is enabled. The source code did not change; the compiler configuration did.

First prize: a clean build. Second prize: steak knives. Compiler errors are cheaper than runtime failures.
3

TypeScript deeper: interfaces, generics and inference

This is where the type system starts to feel like a design tool instead of just annotations on variables.

Extend interfaces

Extending interfaces 
interface BaseRecord {{
  readonly id: number;
  createdAt: string;
}}

interface Attempt extends BaseRecord {{
  username: string;
  outcome: string;
  notes?: string;
}}

readonly is compiler-enforced. ? makes a property optional.

Interfaces can include behavior

Method signature 
interface Verifier {{
  verify(username: string): boolean;
}}

An interface can describe methods as well as data.

Generic functions

Generic function 
function first<T>(
  items: T[]
): T | undefined {{
  return items[0];
}}

T stands in for the element type. The compiler can infer T from the argument.

Generic interfaces

Result<T> 
interface Result<T> {{
  success: boolean;
  value?: T;
  error?: string;
}}

A single wrapper can carry a success value of any type without giving up type information.

Constrained generics

Constrained generic 
function describeByUsername<
  T extends {{ username: string }}
>(record: T): string {{
  return `Record for ${{record.username}}`;
}}

Any shape is accepted as long as it contains at least a username: string property.

Structural typing: TypeScript checks whether the required shape is present. Java generics are nominal: a bounded type normally has to implement the declared interface explicitly.
Lab starter: report.ts

Quiz hint

An empty interface does not magically add safety. If it declares no required properties, many object shapes can satisfy it. Also remember that TypeScript's generic constraints are shape-based.

4

Node.js fundamentals: who is actually running the room?

Node is more than “JavaScript on the server.” It combines the V8 engine, libuv and Node-specific APIs.

First prize

V8 + libuv + Node APIs

V8 executes JavaScript. libuv provides event-loop and async-I/O infrastructure. Node adds APIs such as fs, http, process and CommonJS require().

Second prize

Know the event loop order

JavaScript code executes on the call stack one frame at a time. Async work completes elsewhere, then callbacks are queued until the event loop can move them back onto the stack.

The call order on the board

1. SyncOrdinary code on the call stack runs first.
2. nextTickIn the CommonJS example, Node drains process.nextTick callbacks.
3. Promise microtasksPromise.then callbacks are drained before macrotasks.
4. MacrotasksetTimeout callbacks run only after the earlier queues are ready.
CommonJS event-loop example 
console.log("1: synchronous");

setTimeout(
  () => console.log("5: setTimeout"),
  0
);

Promise.resolve().then(
  () => console.log("4: Promise.then")
);

process.nextTick(
  () => console.log("3: process.nextTick")
);

console.log("2: synchronous");
Verified surprise: the supplied module notes show the same snippet producing a different nextTick/Promise ordering when run as an ES module under the tested Node version. Treat simplified queue-order slogans as rules of thumb, not universal laws.

CommonJS

CommonJS 
function isKnownUser(username) {{
  return KNOWN_USERS.includes(username);
}}

module.exports = {{
  isKnownUser,
  KNOWN_USERS
}};

const {{ isKnownUser }} =
  require("./verify-utils.cjs");

module.exports exposes one object. require() is synchronous and may be called conditionally.

ES Modules

ES Modules 
export function isKnownUser(username) {{
  return KNOWN_USERS.includes(username);
}}

import {{
  isKnownUser
}} from "./verify-utils.mjs";

ESM uses per-declaration export and static import. Node's ESM rules are also why explicit extensions matter in NodeNext TypeScript builds.

package.json

Defines package metadata, scripts, dependency ranges and module type. dependencies ship with the app; devDependencies support building or testing.

Semver

^7.0.2 allows compatible updates without a major bump. ~7.0.2 stays within patch-level updates. No prefix pins the version exactly.

package-lock.json

The lockfile records the exact resolved dependency tree, including transitive dependencies, so installs reproduce the same versions across machines.

Quiz hint

Know the difference between the JavaScript call stack, libuv work, microtasks and macrotasks. Also know CommonJS versus ES Modules: module.exports/require() is not just alternate spelling for export/import.

5

The labs: prove it instead of memorizing it

Each exercise is built around a real compiler or runtime behavior that students can predict, run and verify.

Lab 6: fix the build

Add module: "NodeNext", moduleResolution: "NodeNext" and strict: true, then watch a broken import move from runtime failure to compile-time error.

Target output: dave is verified

Lab 7: extend, generalize, constrain

Build BaseRecord, LoginAttempt, Result<T> and a constrained generic describeByUsername.

The interesting question is what TypeScript checks when two unrelated object shapes both satisfy the same generic constraint.

Lab 8: modules and event loop

Implement countByOutcome using CommonJS, then predict the sync/nextTick/Promise/setTimeout print order before running it.

Expected count: 2 successful, 2 failed.

count-utils.cjs

}

report.cjs 
// KATA: run this now, before changing anything:
//   node report.cjs
// It throws at TODO 1 (inside count-utils.cjs). That's the starting
// point.

const { countByOutcome } = require("./count-utils.cjs");

const attempts = [
  { username: "dave", outcome: "success" },
  { username: "erin", outcome: "fail" },
  { username: "dave", outcome: "fail" },
  { username: "frank", outcome: "success" },
];

const { successCount, failCount } = countByOutcome(attempts);
console.log(`${successCount} successful, ${failCount} failed`);

// TODO 2: before running this section, PREDICT the print order on paper

// console.log("sync A");

Best habit in this section: predict first, run second. Compiler messages and runtime ordering are much more useful when they confirm or contradict a concrete expectation you had before execution.
Always be compiling. Always be checking. By the end of this section, TypeScript should feel like a compiler you can reason about, Node should feel like a runtime you can explain, and the move into NestJS should feel like the next sales meeting rather than a mysterious new language.
